original: Three-dimensional object detection from Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) point clouds is critical for autonomous navigation; however, conventional volumetric and pillar-based architectures impose severe computational challenges on edge accelerators. We propose MobilePIXORNeXt, an ultra-compact, proposal-free Bird's-Eye View (BEV) detector operating under 753,569 parameters. The framework replaces learned point encoders with Strata-BEV14, a parameter-free deterministic NumPy/Numba CPU rasterizer that extracts 14 statistical feature channels---capturing stratified height distributions, elevation moments, surface reflectance, and continuous subcell centroid displacement offsets---with a measured input preprocessing time of 20.94 milliseconds, including point-cloud loading and rasterization. Spatial features are extracted by a single-branch ConvNeXt-style backbone with embedded parameter-free 3D spatial-energy attention (Block-SimAM), fused through a Scale-Gated Feature Pyramid Network, and predicted by decoupled grouped heads. Training is supervised by Physics-Consistent Ground-Truth Augmentation and Oriented Geometric Alignment, dynamically balanced via 12-parameter Temperature-Softmax Bounded Uncertainty Weighting. On the KITTI validation set using BEV AP $R_{40}$, MobilePIXORNeXt achieves 71.46\% Moderate mean Average Precision (mAP) and 73.42\% overall 9-cell mAP across Car, Pedestrian, and Cyclist categories. It outperforms PointPillars (70.13\% mAP) with an 84.4\% parameter reduction and matches SECOND (72.09\% mAP) with 85.8\% fewer parameters, while reaching 60.75\% Moderate AP on pedestrians. The complete pipeline executes in 60.96 milliseconds (16.41 frames per second) on an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, delivering the fastest end-to-end throughput among evaluated real-time detectors. Our findings demonstrate that deterministic statistical encoding and oriented geometric supervision enable high-accuracy LiDAR perception on resource-constrained embedded systems.

original: Three-dimensional (3D) spatial perception from Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) point clouds provides essential sensory grounding for safe autonomous navigation, mobile robotics, and intelligent transportation systems. Unlike passive optical cameras, which remain vulnerable to ambient illumination fluctuations and projective scale ambiguities, LiDAR sensors actively emit pulsed laser beams to measure direct metric ranges, capturing high-precision geometric boundaries under arbitrary day-and-night conditions~\cite{geiger2012kitti}. In time-critical vehicular environments, perception systems must accurately detect, orient, and classify surrounding objects (from passenger vehicles to compact vulnerable road users such as pedestrians and cyclists) within strict latency envelopes, typically requiring sub-$100\,\text{ms}$ execution per scan~\cite{yang2018pixor}. However, deploying high-accuracy 3D object detection models on embedded vehicular platforms faces an acute operational tension between detection accuracy and hardware resource consumption. Commodity onboard edge accelerators operate under stringent thermal and electrical power budgets, where memory bandwidth, cache capacity, and arithmetic throughput are strictly constrained. Consequently, developing ultra-compact yet highly discriminative LiDAR object detection architectures that sustain real-time execution without forfeiting spatial localization fidelity remains an essential prerequisite for scalable autonomous driving.

original: To extract 3D bounding boxes from unstructured point clouds, existing detection paradigms fall into three primary methodological families, each exhibiting inherent architectural trade-offs on resource-constrained platforms. First, volumetric voxel-based architectures, exemplified by SECOND~\cite{yan2018second}, and two-stage point-voxel frameworks, such as PointRCNN~\cite{shi2019pointrcnn}, Part-$A^2$~\cite{shi2020part}, and PV-RCNN~\cite{shi2020pvrcnn}, achieve competitive detection accuracy by deploying 3D sparse convolutions or localized point-cloud abstractions. Nevertheless, their multi-million parameter footprints ($4.0\text{--}63.8\,\text{M}$) and heavy memory access latencies ($100\text{--}195\,\text{ms}$) exceed the operational limits of embedded edge processors. Second, pillar-based detectors, pioneered by PointPillars~\cite{lang2019pointpillars} and modernized by PillarNeXt~\cite{li2023pillarnext} and PillarNeSt~\cite{mao2023pillarnest}, project points into vertical pillars processed via PointNet encoders to construct Bird's-Eye View (BEV) 2D feature representations. While faster than volumetric methods, non-deterministic point gathering, dynamic memory allocation, and sparse scattering introduce substantial runtime overhead and memory transfer latency. Third, proposal-free BEV rasterization methods, such as PIXOR~\cite{yang2018pixor} and MobilePIXOR~\cite{nguyen2024indoor}, eliminate learned encoders entirely by discretizing point clouds into fixed vertical occupancy grids. Although conceptually efficient, existing rasterization methods suffer from severe spatial quantization errors on standard $0.1\,\text{m}$ grids; by relying on crude binary occupancy slices, they discard continuous subcell offsets and high-order vertical dispersion statistics, inducing spatial staircasing and localization jitter on small objects. While recent studies such as PillarHist~\cite{zhou2025pillarhist} explore height histograms and TriBand-BEV~\cite{khoshkdahan2026triband} explores multi-band vertical slicing, they still omit continuous subcell displacements combined with continuous vertical spatial moments. In addition, naive cut-and-paste data augmentation creates physical artifacts, small-scale backbones experience receptive-field starvation across disparate object dimensions, and uncalibrated classification heatmaps cause misaligned false positives to suppress well-localized candidates during Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)~\cite{li2020gfl}. The failure of existing compact detectors to simultaneously resolve fine subcell quantization errors, unphysical augmentation artifacts, multi-scale receptive field coverage, and geometric score misalignment constitutes the core bottleneck impeding sub-million-parameter LiDAR perception.

original: We address this fundamental challenge through a key scientific insight: sub-voxel geometric precision can be preserved deterministically at the representation level by coupling multi-band vertical densities and continuous elevation moments with horizontal subcell centroid displacements, bypassing learned PointNet encoders entirely without forfeiting fine spatial boundaries. Grounded in this principle, we investigate the central research question: \textit{Can an ultra-compact LiDAR detector operating on a parameter-free BEV tensor rival the localization accuracy of heavy volumetric and pillar architectures while achieving superior end-to-end throughput on commodity edge hardware?} To realize this objective, our framework couples this deterministic representation with a single-branch ConvNeXt-style backbone~\cite{liu2022convnext} utilizing large $7 \times 7$ depthwise kernels and parameter-free 3D spatial-energy attention (SimAM)~\cite{yang2021simam}, expanding physical receptive fields to envelop entire vehicles without multi-branch training overhead. Concurrently, physics-consistent data synthesis regularizes distant returns, while multi-axis geometric supervision and localization-quality ranking align backpropagation gradients directly with rotated bounding box overlap. Together, these complementary mechanisms demonstrate that disciplined geometric encoding and calibrated multi-task loss formulation bridge the performance divide between compact 2D representations and multi-million-parameter 3D networks.

original: Dense horizontal projection provides an efficient pathway to apply high-throughput 2D convolutional networks to unstructured 3D LiDAR point clouds. PIXOR~\cite{yang2018pixor} established the foundational paradigm of proposal-free Bird's-Eye View (BEV) detection by discretizing point clouds into fixed vertical occupancy slices and calibrated reflectance maps. Building upon this formulation, Nguyen et al.~\cite{nguyen2024indoor} introduced MobilePIXOR, replacing heavyweight convolutional layers with inverted residual blocks and Gaussian heatmap supervision for indoor robotic perception. In parallel, PointPillars~\cite{lang2019pointpillars} eliminated rigid vertical slicing by organizing point clouds into vertical columns (pillars) and learning spatial feature representations via localized PointNet encoders. Modern extensions such as PillarNeXt~\cite{li2023pillarnext} and PillarNeSt~\cite{mao2023pillarnest} systematically modernized pillar-based receptive field designs and backbone scaling for large-scale outdoor perception.

original: A fundamental operational dichotomy divides existing BEV representations between expressive PointNet-based pillar feature encoders and high-speed fixed-grid rasterization. On one hand, PointNet-based pillar encoders~\cite{lang2019pointpillars,li2023pillarnext} achieve expressive geometric learning, yet the non-deterministic point gathering, dynamic memory allocation, and sparse scatter operations incur prohibitive latency and energy penalties on edge accelerators. On the other hand, fixed-grid rasterization methods~\cite{yang2018pixor,nguyen2024indoor} bypass point gathering entirely but suffer from severe spatial quantization error on standard $0.1\,\text{m}$ grids; by treating cells as binary flags or raw counters, they discard continuous subcell offsets and high-order vertical distributions, causing boundary staircasing and localization jitter. While recent studies such as PillarHist~\cite{zhou2025pillarhist} investigate quantization-aware height histograms and TriBand-BEV~\cite{khoshkdahan2026triband} explores multi-band vertical slicing to assist pedestrian detection, a shared limitation across these paradigms is the absence of continuous subcell centroid displacements coupled with continuous vertical statistical moments inside a compact, hardware-friendly tensor. MobilePIXORNeXt overcomes this limitation through the Strata-BEV14 representation (Section~\ref{sec:strata_bev14}). By deterministically integrating four stratified vertical density bins, four continuous elevation moments ($\mu_z, \sigma_z, z_{\min}, z_{\max}$), and two continuous subcell centroid displacement offsets ($\Delta x_c, \Delta y_c$) into a 14-channel layout, Strata-BEV14 preserves sub-voxel geometric fidelity while reducing Host-to-Device transfer payloads by $60\%$ without learned encoder latency.
revised: BEV representations commonly use either learned PointNet-based pillar encoders or fixed-grid rasterization. Pillar encoders~\cite{lang2019pointpillars,li2023pillarnext} learn geometric features but require point gathering, dynamic memory allocation, and sparse scattering, which add latency and energy costs on edge accelerators. Fixed-grid methods~\cite{yang2018pixor,nguyen2024indoor} avoid learned point encoding. However, binary flags or raw cell counts on $0.1\,\text{m}$ grids omit continuous subcell offsets and higher-order vertical distributions, causing boundary staircasing and localization jitter. PillarHist~\cite{zhou2025pillarhist} investigated quantization-aware height histograms, and TriBand-BEV~\cite{khoshkdahan2026triband} explored multi-band vertical slicing for pedestrian detection. These methods do not combine continuous subcell centroid displacements with continuous vertical statistical moments in a compact tensor. MobilePIXORNeXt uses Strata-BEV14 (Section~\ref{sec:strata_bev14}) to combine four stratified density bins, four continuous elevation moments ($\mu_z, \sigma_z, z_{\min}, z_{\max}$), and two subcell centroid displacement offsets ($\Delta x_c, \Delta y_c$). This 14-channel layout preserves sub-voxel geometry. Strata-BEV14 also reduces Host-to-Device transfer payloads by $60\%$ without a learned encoder.

original: Extracting discriminative spatial semantics from sparse BEV feature planes requires balancing expressive receptive fields with strict parameter and latency constraints. In 3D LiDAR perception, volumetric detectors such as SECOND~\cite{yan2018second} popularized sparse convolutions to process non-empty voxels, while two-stage point architectures such as PointRCNN~\cite{shi2019pointrcnn} and hybrid frameworks such as Part-$A^2$~\cite{shi2020part} and PV-RCNN~\cite{shi2020pvrcnn} introduced part-aware aggregation and voxel-set abstractions. Although these methods achieve high detection accuracy on benchmarks such as KITTI~\cite{geiger2012kitti}, their multi-million parameter footprints ($4.0\text{--}63.8\,\text{M}$) and heavy memory access latencies ($130\text{--}195\,\text{ms}$) prohibit real-time deployment on power-constrained edge accelerators.

PointRCNN~\cite{shi2019pointrcnn}, Part-$A^2$~\cite{shi2020part}, and PV-RCNN~\cite{shi2020pvrcnn} developed two-stage point processing, part-aware aggregation, and voxel-set abstractions. These methods achieve high accuracy on KITTI~\cite{geiger2012kitti}, but their parameter counts ($4.0\text{--}63.8\,\text{M}$) and memory access latencies ($130\text{--}195\,\text{ms}$) limit real-time use on power-constrained edge accelerators.

original: To overcome the latency bottleneck of volumetric processing, lightweight 2D convolutional designs have gained prominence. The ConvNeXt paradigm~\cite{liu2022convnext} demonstrated that conventional convolutions modernized with $7 \times 7$ depthwise kernels, inverted bottleneck expansions ($e=2.5$), and LayerScale can achieve representational power competitive with Vision Transformers while preserving convolutional hardware efficiency. Concurrently, lightweight attention mechanisms have been developed to emphasize salient geometric features. While Efficient Channel Attention (ECA-Net)~\cite{wang2020eca} captures 1D cross-channel interactions with low complexity, it lacks spatial feature modulation. To address this weakness, Yang et al.~\cite{yang2021simam} proposed SimAM, deriving full 3D spatial-channel attention weights analytically via an energy function inspired by visual neuroscience, requiring zero trainable parameters.
revised: Lightweight 2D convolutions offer an alternative to volumetric processing. It demonstrated accuracy competitive with Vision Transformers while retaining convolutional hardware efficiency. Lightweight attention mechanisms further modulate geometric features. Efficient Channel Attention (ECA-Net)~\cite{wang2020eca} modeled 1D cross-channel interactions with low complexity but did not modulate individual spatial locations. Yang et al.~\cite{yang2021simam} proposed SimAM, deriving 3D spatial-channel attention analytically from an energy function inspired by visual neuroscience, without trainable parameters.

original: Collectively, a shared limitation of prior mobile LiDAR detectors is the reliance on standard inverted residual bottlenecks with small $3 \times 3$ kernels~\cite{nguyen2024indoor}, which struggle to capture multi-scale context across disparate vehicle and pedestrian dimensions. Additionally, attempting to compensate by appending external attention modules or distillation schemes at coarse downsampling boundaries~\cite{tran2026rubber} introduces architectural overhead without resolving intra-block receptive field bottlenecks under sparse point distributions. In contrast, MobilePIXORNeXt incorporates the MobilePixorNeXt-S backbone with embedded parameter-free Block-SimAM (Sections~\ref{sec:backbone_architecture}--\ref{sec:next_s_block}) and a Top-Down Scale-Gated FPN (Section~\ref{sec:neck_architecture}), capturing expansive $7 \times 7$ depthwise receptive fields and modulating residual feature updates directly inside every residual block with zero added attention parameters.

original: Bounding box regression in oriented object detection has progressively evolved from unconstrained coordinate offsets toward geometrically bounded objectives. Early detectors primarily relied on decoupled Smooth-L1 loss functions. However, regressing spatial coordinates, dimensions, and angles independently ignores the geometric interdependence of bounding boxes and induces severe gradient instability. To provide scale-invariant geometric feedback, Rezatofighi et al.~\cite{rezatofighi2019giou} introduced Generalized Intersection over Union (GIoU) to address gradient vanishing when candidate bounding boxes do not overlap. More recently, Le et al.~\cite{le2026mgiou} formulated Marginalized Generalized Intersection over Union (MGIoU), establishing a unified projection-based framework to optimize convex parametric shapes and arbitrary oriented bounding boxes without rotational singularities.
revised: Oriented bounding box regression has developed from independent coordinate losses toward geometric objectives. Early detectors used decoupled Smooth-L1 losses. Independent regression of coordinates, dimensions, and angles ignores their geometric dependence and can destabilize gradients. Rezatofighi et al.~\cite{rezatofighi2019giou} introduced Generalized Intersection over Union (GIoU) to provide scale-invariant feedback when boxes do not overlap. Le et al.~\cite{le2026mgiou} later formulated Marginalized Generalized Intersection over Union (MGIoU), a projection-based objective for convex parametric shapes and arbitrarily oriented boxes without rotational singularities.

original: In parallel with geometric loss formulation, joint quality calibration has emerged as an essential mechanism for accurate detection ranking. Li et al.~\cite{li2020gfl} introduced Generalized Focal Loss (GFL), demonstrating that uncalibrated classification scores frequently disagree with actual localization quality, causing low-quality boxes with high confidence to suppress well-localized candidates during Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS). Additionally, Kendall et al.~\cite{kendall2018uncertainty} introduced multi-task uncertainty weighting, utilizing homoscedastic task variance to balance heterogeneous loss objectives across classification and geometric regression tasks.
revised: Localization quality calibration also affects detection ranking. Li et al.~\cite{li2020gfl} introduced Generalized Focal Loss (GFL). They showed that classification scores can disagree with localization quality, allowing high-confidence but poorly localized boxes to suppress accurate candidates during Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS). Kendall et al.~\cite{kendall2018uncertainty} introduced multi-task uncertainty weighting to balance classification and geometric regression losses through homoscedastic task variance.

original: Despite these advancements, existing oriented bounding box detectors still struggle with three pervasive limitations. First, independent angle and corner regression objectives remain susceptible to the $\pi$-periodicity boundary jump problem, where slight angular deviations around $\pm \pi/2$ or $\pm \pi$ trigger severe loss spikes and yaw gradient collapse. Second, conventional quality calibration mechanisms rely on auxiliary decoupled prediction heads that inflate model parameters and exacerbate gradient contention across heterogeneous object classes. Third, unconstrained multi-task uncertainty weighting allows task variance parameters to diverge, leading to training instability when balancing disparate loss scales across classification, geometric overlap, and orientation. MobilePIXORNeXt addresses these multi-task supervision bottlenecks through a unified framework combining Oriented Geometric Alignment (OGA), its head-free alternative Q-OGA, and IoU-Aware Quality Alignment (IQA) (Section~\ref{sec:losses_and_oga}). Specifically, OGA unifies multi-axis MGIoU projections with scale-normalized $\pi$-symmetric corner supervision to eliminate boundary discontinuities; Q-OGA couples continuous IoU quality directly into classification supervision to achieve quality calibration with zero head overhead; IQA provides explicit multi-branch quality alignment scored via $S_{\mathrm{det}} = \sqrt{P_{\mathrm{cls}}\hat{q}}$ to suppress miscalibrated false positives; and Temperature-Softmax Bounded Uncertainty Weighting (T-SBUW) guarantees stable convergence by constraining multi-task weights within a normalized, bounded simplex, simultaneously resolving orientation discontinuities, quality miscalibration, and loss scale divergence.
revised: Three supervision limitations remain in oriented detection. Independent angle and corner losses are sensitive to the $\pi$-periodicity boundary: small angular deviations near $\pm \pi/2$ or $\pm \pi$ can cause loss spikes and unstable yaw gradients. Auxiliary quality heads add parameters and can increase gradient competition across classes. Unconstrained uncertainty weights can also diverge when classification, overlap, and orientation losses have different scales. MobilePIXORNeXt combines Oriented Geometric Alignment (OGA), its head-free alternative Q-OGA, and IoU-Aware Quality Alignment (IQA) (Section~\ref{sec:losses_and_oga}) to address these issues. OGA combines multi-axis MGIoU projections with scale-normalized $\pi$-symmetric corner supervision to avoid orientation boundary discontinuities. Q-OGA incorporates continuous IoU quality into classification supervision without an additional head. IQA provides explicit multi-branch quality prediction and uses $S_{\mathrm{det}} = \sqrt{P_{\mathrm{cls}}\hat{q}}$ to rank detections. Temperature-Softmax Bounded Uncertainty Weighting (T-SBUW) constrains task weights to a normalized, bounded simplex to limit loss scale imbalance during optimization.

original: The proposed MobilePIXORNeXt architecture processes 14-channel Strata-BEV14 tensors. Parameter-free Block-SimAM attention is embedded inside all nine residual blocks. The multiscale Scale-Gated Feature Pyramid Network (SG-FPN) fuses stages C4, C3, and C2 into an optimal $F_{32}$ (32-channel) representation at stride 4 ($200 \times 176$). Decoupled GroupedHeader towers process Car ($K_1=1$) and Pedestrian/Cyclist ($K_2=2$) independently, utilizing a shared initial $3 \times 3$ Conv-BN-SiLU transformation per group. original: The empirical results indicate that high-accuracy 3D LiDAR object detection does not strictly necessitate parameter-heavy point-cloud encoders or computationally demanding 3D sparse convolutions. By enriching the deterministic 2D BEV representation with multi-band vertical densities, elevation dispersion moments, and continuous subcell centroid displacements, a streamlined ConvNeXt-style 2D convolutional network extracts expressive geometric features with fewer than $0.76\,\text{M}$ parameters. In addition, enforcing physical realism in data augmentation (\texttt{PC-GTA}) and resolving multi-task gradient competition through decoupled grouped heads provided larger empirical performance gains than model depth scaling alone.

Physics-consistent augmentation (\texttt{PC-GTA}) and decoupled grouped heads produced larger observed accuracy gains than model depth scaling alone.

original: The current MobilePIXORNeXt architecture operates primarily on oriented 2D Bird's-Eye View footprints ($x, y, l, w, \psi$), which represents the optimal perception trade-off for autonomous vehicle motion planning and collision avoidance under strict edge-computing power envelopes. Although 3D bounding box estimation ($z, h$) is supported via our optional vertical prediction head, full 3D height estimation on heavily sloped terrains remains an active area of investigation. Future research will explore range-conditioned frequency modulations (RC-SGFPN) and hardware-specific TensorRT INT8 quantization for ultra-low-power micro-mobility microcontrollers.
